props.title: Faraway, So Close!
props.initialSlug: Angel yearns for human life in divided Berlin.

sections.content: Wim Wenders' ambitious sequel to Wings of Desire (1987) continues the story of angels watching over Berlin, but with a distinctly post-Wall perspective. While its predecessor captured a divided city's melancholy, Faraway, So Close! (1993) grapples with reunification's chaos and promise. The film follows Cassiel (Otto Sander), who, inspired by former angel Damiel's example, chooses to become human. But where Damiel found love and purpose, Cassiel struggles with human vices and Berlin's criminal underworld. Wenders weaves a complex tapestry that includes Lou Reed, Willem Dafoe as a mysterious time-traveling figure, and Nastassja Kinski as an angel - creating a meditation on freedom's price that's both more ambitious and messier than the original.

sections.content: The film represents a crucial moment in German cinema's attempt to process reunification. While films like Good Bye, Lenin! (2003) would later approach the subject with nostalgic humor, Wenders tackles it head-on through metaphysical allegory. The angel-turned-human narrative becomes a powerful metaphor for East Germans suddenly thrust into capitalism's freedoms and temptations. This theme resonates with other post-Wall German films like The Lives of Others (2006), though Wenders' approach is more experimental and spiritually focused. SUBHEAD: Angels in Cinema and Urban Spaces

Faraway, So Close! belongs to a unique subset of films exploring urban spaces through supernatural observers. While different in tone, City of Angels (1998) borrowed Wings of Desire's premise for a Hollywood romance. Michael Winterbottom's Wonderland (1999) adopted a similar hovering perspective over London, though without literal angels. Wenders' angels serve as witnesses to history, similar to how the ghost in A Matter of Life and Death (1946) observes post-war Britain.
